sections.normalized_html: Determine the number of distinct real solutions for the equation [MATH: 2t^{2} + 5t + 1 = 0.]
sections.readable_text: Determine the number of distinct real solutions for the equation [MATH: 2t^{2} + 5t + 1 = 0.]

sections.normalized_html:
For a quadratic equation [MATH: at^2 + bt + c = 0,] the discriminant is [MATH: \mathcal{D} = b^2 - 4ac.]

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} > 0,] there are two distinct real solutions.

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0,] there is exactly one real solution.

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0,] there are no real solutions (the solutions are complex).

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

[MATH: a = 2, \qquad b = 5, \qquad c = 1]

So, the discriminant is

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = 5^{2} − 4(2)(1); = 25 − 8; = 17.]

Since the discriminant is positive ([MATH: \mathcal{D} > 0]), the quadratic equation has exactly two real solutions.

sections.normalized_html:
To determine how many times the graph of [MATH: y=ax^2-b] intersects the graph of [MATH: y=a+2b,] we must find the [MATH: x]-coordinates of such points (if any). To do this, we equate the [MATH: y]-values ​​of both equations, as follows: [MATH: a x^2 - b = a + 2b]

Next, we isolate the [MATH: x^2] on one side of the equation: [MATH: ax^{2} − b|= a + 2b; ax^{2}|= a + 3b; x^{2}|= (a + 3b)/(a)]

Note that the last operation is possible since [MATH: a] is positive. Also note that [MATH: \dfrac{a + 3b}{a}] is positive. Thus, we can take the square root of both sides of the last equation and solve the resulting absolute value equation: [MATH: x^{2}|= (a + 3b)/(a); sqrt(x^{2})|= sqrt((a + 3b)/(a));|x||= sqrt((a + 3b)/(a)); x|= ± sqrt((a + 3b)/(a))]

Therefore, we can conclude that the graph of [MATH: y = a x^{2} - b] intersects the graph of [MATH: y = a + 2b] exactly twice.
